name: Oiling and massaging newborns
what_people_do: Rub cooking oil, other natural oils or petroleum jelly into a newborn after bathing; massage the belly with a kola paste in some Nigerian communities.
why_they_say_it_works: To keep the baby's skin supple, strengthen the limbs and, in the kola-paste custom, prevent thrush and skin infection.

documented_by.source: Postnatal care and emollient therapy, Harare, 2024, BMC Pediatr, PMID 38493088
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Harare, 61 mothers interviewed: postnatal skincare is central, petroleum jelly application is nearly universal, and cooking oil and other natural oils are traditional.

documented_by.source: Iweze FA 1983, J Nurse Midwifery, PMID 6552278 (Bendel State, Nigeria)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Bendel State, Nigeria (1983 ethnographic outline): mothers make a paste of kola nuts and rub it on the abdomen to prevent thrush and skin infection in the newborn; midwives do abdominal massage.

evidence.tested: Emollient therapy in preterm or low-birth-weight babies
evidence.population: WHO recommendation cited in the abstract; trials not opened
evidence.finding: The abstract says WHO recommends emollient therapy for preterm and low-birth-weight infants and calls for more research in Africa.

source.name: Postnatal care and emollient therapy, Harare, 2024, BMC Pediatr, PMID 38493088
agent4-traditional-practices.md, 12 Nov 2026 (research file in this project)

harm_note: Oils can irritate and some cooking oils may harm fragile skin (not sourced here); for preterm babies clinics now offer emollient therapy.
gaps: Trial-level evidence for emollients not opened.
Which oils are best for dark-skinned newborns not found.
